<span id="top"></span>

A **graph** is a way to represent entities and the relationships between them. The entities are called **nodes** and their relationships are called **edges**. Both may carry useful information: a customer node might contain age or location, a product node might contain category and price, and an edge might record that a customer bought or rated a product. Road sensors connected by roads, transactions linked by payments and atoms connected by chemical bonds are other examples.

![A small customer-product graph. Solid edges are observed purchases; the dashed edge is a possible recommendation.](assets/customer-product-graph.svg){.graph-example fig-alt="Three customer nodes connected to three product nodes. Solid edges represent purchases and one dashed edge represents a possible recommendation."}

A **graph neural network (GNN)** learns numerical representations, or embeddings, by combining a node's own features with information from its neighbours. In the example, the model can use a customer's previous purchases, the properties of products and patterns from nearby customers to score a new customer-product link. The same principle supports **node classification** (classify a transaction), **link prediction** (recommend a product), and **graph-level prediction** (predict a property of an entire molecule or sensor system).

Each project below asks a specific question about *when and why* the graph helps — not simply whether a GNN can be trained. Students define what the nodes and edges mean, fix a split and a primary metric, and always include a control that tests whether the graph contributes at all.

::: {.category-callout}
**Application project requirements**

Specify a defensible graph construction, a fixed split and primary metric, a non-graph baseline and at least one GNN. Include an edge-removal, edge-randomisation or alternative-graph experiment to test whether the graph contributes.
:::

## Learn first and find ideas

- Begin with [A Gentle Introduction to Graph Neural Networks](https://distill.pub/2021/gnn-intro/), then use the [Stanford CS224W course and project guidance](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224w/projects.html) and the [CS224W project archive](https://snap.stanford.edu/class/cs224w-2019/projects.html).
- [PyTorch Geometric dataset catalogue](https://pytorch-geometric.readthedocs.io/en/latest/cheatsheet/data_cheatsheet.html), [Open Graph Benchmark](https://ogb.stanford.edu/docs/home/), [SNAP datasets](https://snap.stanford.edu/data/) and the [Temporal Graph Benchmark](https://tgb.complexdatalab.com/).
- Stanford examples: [traffic as a dynamic graph](https://medium.com/stanford-cs224w/predicting-evolution-of-dynamic-graphs-7688eca1daf8), [water quality with RGCNs](https://medium.com/stanford-cs224w/predicting-water-quality-in-unmonitored-networks-with-rgcns-c72fdd177f0d), [fake-news detection](https://medium.com/stanford-cs224w/are-you-for-real-cb0442af43a3) and [NFT transaction prediction](https://medium.com/stanford-cs224w/applying-graph-ml-techniques-to-ethereum-nft-transactions-d4bde61b02f3).

## 1.1  Remaining useful life prediction for aircraft engines {#project-1-1}

::: {.project-meta}
<span class="meta-label">Task</span><span class="meta-value">Graph-level temporal regression</span>
<span class="meta-label">Level</span><span class="meta-value">BSc or MSc</span>
<span class="meta-label">Compute</span><span class="meta-value">Very light to light; CPU or 4 GB GPU</span>
<span class="meta-label">Data</span><span class="meta-value">[NASA C-MAPSS](https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/cmapss-jet-engine-simulated-data) — FD001: 100 training engines, 100 test engines, 21 sensor channels</span>
<span class="meta-label">Starting paper</span><span class="meta-value">Huang, He and Sick, [Spatio-Temporal Attention GNN for RUL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15964), 2024</span>
:::

::: {.project-intro}
**What you will do.** Predict how many operating cycles remain before a turbofan engine fails. Each sensor channel becomes a node and edges express relationships among sensors. The project's real subject is the graph itself: does it matter how you connect the sensors?
:::

**Data.** Start with FD001; FD002–FD004 are optional transfer sets. Split by **engine**, never by windows from the same engine, and fit normalisation and graph construction on training engines only.

**Methods and code.** A GRU, LSTM or TCN as the graph-free baseline, and a compact GCN–GRU or GAT–GRU as the graph model. [PHMGNNBenchmark](https://github.com/HazeDT/PHMGNNBenchmark) and the [GNN RUL benchmarking repository](https://github.com/Frank-Wang-oss/GNN_RUL_Benchmarking) are useful references, but a compact model written directly in [PyTorch Geometric](https://pytorch-geometric.readthedocs.io/) is sufficient.

**Baselines and evaluation.** A naive constant or degradation-stage baseline, one graph-free sequence model and one compact GNN. MAE or RMSE is primary; report error separately for early, middle and late life. Three seeds for MSc work.

::: {.scope .scope-bsc}
**Bachelor research question.** **How sensitive is GNN-based remaining-useful-life prediction to the way the sensor graph is constructed?**

*Core experiment.* Keep the predictive model fixed and vary only the graph: a correlation graph, a k-nearest-neighbour graph over sensor similarity, a random graph, and a no-edge control. Compare all four against the graph-free sequence baseline.

**Expected outcome.** FD001 has only 21 sensor channels, so the graph may carry little information beyond the sequence itself. A result showing that the correlation graph performs no better than a random graph is a valid and informative finding — it tells you the gain came from the temporal model, not the topology. Report it rather than searching for a configuration in which the graph appears to help.
:::

::: {.scope .scope-msc}
**Master research question.** **Can a sparse, time-varying sensor graph improve RUL accuracy and robustness when sensors become noisy or unavailable?** Develop one graph-learning mechanism, compare it against fixed correlation and random graphs at matched capacity, and add a missing-sensor, uncertainty or cross-subset transfer analysis. Rerunning an available implementation is not the contribution.
:::

**Practical notes.** The main risks are window leakage, inconsistent RUL capping and comparing results produced with different normalisation or scoring rules. Freeze these choices before modelling.

## 1.2  Multi-horizon traffic forecasting with data-driven graph structure {#project-1-2}

::: {.project-meta}
<span class="meta-label">Task</span><span class="meta-value">Node-level temporal regression</span>
<span class="meta-label">Level</span><span class="meta-value">BSc or MSc</span>
<span class="meta-label">Compute</span><span class="meta-value">Light to moderate; 4–8 GB GPU</span>
<span class="meta-label">Data</span><span class="meta-value">[METR-LA](https://github.com/liyaguang/DCRNN) — 207 sensors, 34,272 five-minute observations; PEMS-BAY optional</span>
<span class="meta-label">Starting paper</span><span class="meta-value">Wu et al., [Graph WaveNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.00121), IJCAI 2019</span>
:::

::: {.project-intro}
**What you will do.** Forecast traffic speed at every road sensor 15, 30 and 60 minutes ahead, and determine when the road network's structure actually helps. Short-horizon forecasts may depend mostly on a sensor's own recent history, while longer horizons may require information propagating through the network.
:::

**Data.** METR-LA with the established chronological 70/10/20 split. Fit scalers and any correlation graph on the training period only.

**Methods and code.** Historical average and a graph-free GRU as baselines, with [Graph WaveNet](https://github.com/nnzhan/Graph-WaveNet) or STGCN as the spatiotemporal GNN. Prefer these over DCRNN, which is considerably slower to train. Subsampling sensors is an acceptable fallback if training time becomes a problem.

**Baselines and evaluation.** Historical average, graph-free GRU, and the spatiotemporal GNN on the supplied distance graph, plus a randomised-edge and a no-edge control. MAE is primary; also report RMSE and MAPE at each horizon.

::: {.scope .scope-bsc}
**Bachelor research question.** **Does graph information become more valuable as the forecasting horizon increases?**

*Core experiment.* Compare the graph-free model against the spatiotemporal GNN and measure how the gap between them changes from 15 to 30 to 60 minutes, with the randomised-edge control at each horizon.

**One practical point that saves weeks.** A multi-horizon model predicts all three horizons from a **single trained model** — the 12-step output is simply evaluated at different horizon slices. Do not train three separate models.
:::

::: {.scope .scope-msc}
**Master research question.** **Does a time-of-day and traffic-regime-conditioned sparse adjacency improve long-horizon forecasting over both the road graph and a single learned static graph?** Match depth and width, use at least three seeds, and examine whether rush-hour edges differ from free-flow edges and whether learned edges correspond to plausible topology. Keep any dynamic adjacency sparse or low-rank so its cost is explicit; per-timestep dense adjacency is expensive and unstable.
:::

**Practical notes.** This project studies the graph itself. Profile training time early and enforce top-k sparsity if you learn adjacency.

## 1.3  Illicit Bitcoin transaction detection {#project-1-3}

::: {.project-meta}
<span class="meta-label">Task</span><span class="meta-value">Node classification on a temporal graph</span>
<span class="meta-label">Level</span><span class="meta-value">BSc or MSc</span>
<span class="meta-label">Compute</span><span class="meta-value">Light to moderate; the full graph fits on a 4–8 GB GPU</span>
<span class="meta-label">Data</span><span class="meta-value">[Elliptic Bitcoin dataset via PyG](https://pytorch-geometric.readthedocs.io/en/latest/generated/torch_geometric.datasets.EllipticBitcoinTemporalDataset.html) — 203,769 nodes, 234,355 edges, 165 features, 49 time steps</span>
<span class="meta-label">Starting paper</span><span class="meta-value">Weber et al., [Anti-Money Laundering in Bitcoin](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.02591), 2019</span>
:::

::: {.project-intro}
**What you will do.** Each Bitcoin transaction is a node and directed payment flows are edges. Predict whether a labelled transaction is illicit — and find out how much that prediction depends on the payment graph being complete, which in a real investigation it never is.
:::

**Data.** Use the PyG loader, which handles download and the temporal structure. Chronological splits only. Unknown labels are **unlabelled**, not negatives: exclude them from the supervised loss and from metrics. Confirm the dataset's terms of use before publishing results.

**Methods and code.** Logistic regression or gradient boosting on node features; GCN and GraphSAGE from [PyTorch Geometric](https://pytorch-geometric.readthedocs.io/). Use class weighting or focal loss only after establishing an unweighted baseline.

**Baselines and evaluation.** Feature-only classifier, GCN and GraphSAGE, plus a no-edge control. AUPRC or illicit-class F1 is primary; report illicit recall at a fixed false-positive rate and examine performance over time.

::: {.scope .scope-bsc}
**Bachelor research question.** **How robust are GNN-based illicit-transaction detectors when graph information is incomplete?**

*Core experiment.* Train normally, then progressively delete edges at test time — 0%, 10%, 25% and 50% — and identify the point at which neighbourhood information stops contributing. Compare the feature-only model, which is unaffected by edge deletion, against both GNNs.

**Expected outcome.** On this dataset the 165 node features are highly informative, and a gradient-boosting or random-forest model on features alone is a strong competitor to the GNNs. A result showing that features dominate — and that the GNN therefore degrades gracefully because it was never relying much on topology — is expected and is a perfectly good finding. Report it rather than tuning until the GNN wins.
:::

::: {.scope .scope-msc}
**Master research question.** **Can a temporally calibrated GNN remain useful under concept drift and missing transaction edges?** Add one temporal mechanism or uncertainty method, test edge deletion and temporal shift together, and connect threshold choices to realistic investigator workload at a fixed alert budget.
:::

**Practical notes.** Random splitting makes this task unrealistically easy. Keep time ordering, label handling and threshold selection identical across methods.

## 1.4  Graph-based movie recommendation with accuracy and coverage {#project-1-4}

::: {.project-meta}
<span class="meta-label">Task</span><span class="meta-value">Link prediction and ranking on a bipartite graph</span>
<span class="meta-label">Level</span><span class="meta-value">BSc recommended — the MSc route is narrow, see below</span>
<span class="meta-label">Compute</span><span class="meta-value">Very light; CPU or low-memory GPU</span>
<span class="meta-label">Data</span><span class="meta-value">[MovieLens 100K](https://grouplens.org/datasets/movielens/100k/) — 100,000 timestamped ratings, ~1,000 users, ~1,700 movies, 5 MB</span>
<span class="meta-label">Starting paper</span><span class="meta-value">He et al., [LightGCN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.02126), SIGIR 2020</span>
:::

::: {.project-intro}
**What you will do.** Represent users and movies as two node types with interactions as edges, then recommend a ranked list of films. The interesting part is not only whether the recommendations are accurate, but whether they quietly collapse onto a handful of popular titles.
:::

**Data.** Use a per-user chronological split and remove validation and test interactions from the training graph. Keep candidate sets and negative-sampling rules identical across methods.

**Methods and code.** Popularity, item/user nearest neighbours, matrix factorisation and LightGCN. Implementing LightGCN directly in [PyTorch Geometric](https://pytorch-geometric.readthedocs.io/) is simpler than adapting the [official repository](https://github.com/kuandeng/LightGCN), whose data protocol would need reworking for MovieLens 100K anyway.

**Baselines and evaluation.** Popularity and matrix factorisation are mandatory; LightGCN is the graph model. Report NDCG@20 or Recall@20 as primary, **and** catalogue coverage and the average popularity of recommended items.

::: {.scope .scope-bsc}
**Bachelor research question.** **Does graph-based recommendation improve ranking accuracy at the expense of catalogue coverage and long-tail exposure?**

*Core experiment.* Compare popularity, matrix factorisation and LightGCN on both metric families at once, then study one factor — propagation depth or negative sampling — and show how it moves the accuracy/coverage balance.
:::

::: {.scope .scope-msc}
**Master extension (narrow).** A Master project needs a sharper question, such as: **can a calibrated diversity objective improve long-tail exposure without materially reducing NDCG?** This requires user-activity and item-popularity subgroup analysis, multiple seeds and an explicit Pareto trade-off. Without that extension the project belongs at Bachelor level.
:::

**Practical notes.** The principal pitfalls are leakage from future interactions and evaluating on sampled negatives that differ between methods.

## 1.5  Molecular HIV activity prediction with calibrated GNNs {#project-1-5}

::: {.project-meta}
<span class="meta-label">Task</span><span class="meta-value">Graph classification under distribution shift</span>
<span class="meta-label">Level</span><span class="meta-value">BSc or MSc</span>
<span class="meta-label">Compute</span><span class="meta-value">Light to moderate; 4–8 GB GPU</span>
<span class="meta-label">Data</span><span class="meta-value">[OGB ogbg-molhiv](https://ogb.stanford.edu/docs/graphprop/#ogbg-mol) — 41,127 molecular graphs, official scaffold split and evaluator</span>
<span class="meta-label">Starting paper</span><span class="meta-value">Hu et al., [Open Graph Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.00687), NeurIPS 2020</span>
:::

::: {.project-intro}
**What you will do.** A molecule is a graph: atoms are nodes and bonds are edges. Predict whether a molecule is active in the HIV assay — and test whether a learned graph representation generalises to molecular scaffolds it never saw during training better than a decades-old chemical fingerprint does.
:::

**Data.** Use only the official OGB scaffold split and the official evaluator; the [loader guide](https://ogb.stanford.edu/docs/home/) handles download and split indices. **Never compare scaffold-split results against random-split figures.**

**Methods and code.** Morgan fingerprints with logistic regression or random forest via [RDKit](https://www.rdkit.org/); GCN and GIN/GINE from [PyTorch Geometric](https://pytorch-geometric.readthedocs.io/). OGB provides baseline code.

**Baselines and evaluation.** Fingerprint classifier, GCN and GIN/GINE, with one bond-feature or pooling ablation. ROC-AUC is primary; add AUPRC because roughly 3.5% of molecules are active. Three seeds.

::: {.scope .scope-bsc}
**Bachelor research question.** **Do GNNs generalise better than traditional molecular fingerprints to scaffolds not seen during training?**

*Core experiment.* Compare fingerprint and GNN representations on the official scaffold split, and inspect where each fails. If time allows, analyse error as a function of how novel a test scaffold is relative to the training set.

**Expected outcome — read this before you start.** On this benchmark, fingerprints combined with a tree ensemble are known to match or beat plain GCN and GIN. The likely answer to the question is therefore **no**, and that is a genuinely valuable finding: architectural sophistication does not automatically buy generalisation. Do not respond by tuning the GNN until it wins — tuning against a scaffold split is exactly how this evaluation gets silently invalidated.
:::

::: {.scope .scope-msc}
**Master research question.** **Can uncertainty-aware training improve calibration on held-out scaffolds without sacrificing discrimination?** Compare temperature scaling, deep ensembles or a compact evidential variant on identical predictions, and report both performance and calibration as a function of scaffold novelty.
:::

**Practical notes.** The main danger is silently changing the split or selecting a threshold on test data.
